summary: From a computational standpoint the method is cheap. My recomputation reproduces the published RPM point forecasts exactly, and a point forecast costs about 0.03 s on one core. The ground truth and the full benchmark run in under two hours of wall time on 4 cores. Run time is not a barrier for any method, and the paper's conclusion that it is negligible next to a reference analysis is correct. The weaknesses lie in how cost and deployability are reported and supported. (1) The planning rule the paper recommends cannot be applied, because the calibrated band offsets are not published; they exist only transiently inside the analysis script. (2) The only run-time comparison (1.55 s vs 0.52 s) times different work in the two blocks. It hides that about 98% of RPM's cost is a bootstrap that the paper itself shows to under-cover, and that RPM's point forecast is about 12x cheaper than the IPL pipeline. (3) The recommended variant RPM-w is said to 'require only the pilot', but it was evaluated only with up to 12,011 unlabelled spectra. My recomputation shows the claim holds on average, with an n0-dependent trade-off. (4) RPM cannot be reimplemented from the paper: key settings, a user-level interface and an archived code version are missing. (5) The 5-8x wavelength thinning is unexplained, and native-resolution behaviour is untested. Smaller problems concern the timing protocol, bootstrap resolution, a missing dependency and a mislabelled Table 1 column.
strengths: Exact closed-form LOGO ridge paths, kappa by vectorised bisection and a two-parameter fit make an RPM point forecast cost about 0.02-0.03 s per pilot. The complexity is low and dominated by fixed overheads, not by n0.
Run times were actually measured and logged per pilot (raw '_timing' rows; ground-truth seconds in Table S1), not estimated.

The pipeline is deterministic and resumable, runs on CPU only and needs only common scientific-Python packages. Re-running the RPM forecaster on the archived seeds reproduced all 10,700 published RPM forecast values exactly in this review.
The total study compute is modest: main stage 26.7 min wall on 4 cores per the run log. Re-analysis by others is therefore practical.

issues.title: The recommended planning rule cannot be used because the calibrated band offsets are not published
issues.description: The Significance statement, Section 4.5 and recommendation (iii) in Section 4.10 present 'the pilot's cross-validated error, combined with a typical slope and calibrated bands' as the planning rule practitioners should use. The slope is published (8.3% per doubling). The calibrated bands are not: a reader cannot build them from the paper. The leave-one-source-out split-conformal bands are the per-method, per-extrapolation-ratio-bin quantiles of the log errors in the other data sources, subtracted from the forecast. These offsets appear nowhere in the manuscript, the Supplementary Material or results/numbers.json. Only the resulting coverage and the median width factor are reported (Supplementary Table S20 / tables/T16). The procedure exists only as dataframe operations over the benchmark's own raw results inside the analysis script, with no callable function. A practitioner who wants honest bands must download about 1.4 GB of data and rerun the whole 38-task benchmark. The 'factor of about 1.77' quoted in Sections 4.5 and 4.10 is a median width pooled over all pilot sizes and extrapolation ratios. Band width must grow with n/n0, so this single number does not give the band at the ratio a user actually needs. In practice, the only rule the paper gives in usable form is the point forecast. The uncertainty half of the 'sound planning rule' is not deployable.
issues.evidence: code/experiments/analysis.py lines 382-406: the offsets lo_q, hi_q = np.quantile(e, ...) are computed in memory per source and ratio bin and discarded. Only coverage_pct and median_width_factor are written (tables/T16_posthoc_loso_conformal_bands.md; numbers.json['posthoc_conformal']). A grep of supplementary_full.md for 'quantile', 'offset' or 'lookup' finds only the pre-registration line on bootstrap quantiles (line 891). Manuscript Section 4.5 ('Honest 80% bands ... span roughly a factor of 1.77-2.05') and Section 4.10 (iii) give no table. The bins are rbin = round(log2(n/n0)), pooled over n0 = 25-200.
issues.corrective_action: Publish a table of lower and upper log-error offsets (80% and 95%) for SLOPE-T, FLAT and RPM-w, by extrapolation-ratio bin (2, 4, 8, 16, 32+), and by pilot size if this changes the offsets, estimated from all 38 tasks. Also report the leave-one-source-out spread of these offsets so users can judge how stable they are. Provide a small documented function, e.g. plan(pilot_cv_rmse, n0, n_target, method) -> (point, lo80, hi80, lo95, hi95), and one worked numerical example in the main text: pilot of 50 samples, CV-RMSE x, forecast and band at n = 400.

issues.title: The run-time comparison (RPM 1.55 s vs IPL 0.52 s) is not like-for-like and reverses the true cost ordering
issues.description: Section 4.9 and Supplementary Table S31 compare 'an RPM forecast including 50 bootstrap refits' (1.55 s) with '0.52 s to build the within-pilot learning curve that the curve-fitting baselines need'. The two timed blocks contain different work. (a) The RPM block includes 50 Bayesian-bootstrap refits, i.e. the uncertainty bands, but excludes the eigen-decomposition of the unlabelled pool, which is precomputed once per task in run_truth. (b) The IPL block includes only the within-pilot sub-sampling. It excludes the four non-linear curve fits and the delta-method intervals. I re-timed both on the identical 2,640 pilots. My RPM point forecasts reproduce the published ones exactly (max |difference| = 0.0 over 10,700 forecast rows), so the setup matches. Without bootstrap, the RPM point forecast took a median 0.026 s (mean 0.027 s, max 0.14 s). The complete IPL pipeline (sub-sampling plus four curve fits) took a median 0.31 s (mean 0.46 s, max 2.87 s). The RPM point forecast is therefore about 12x cheaper than the curve-fitting baselines, not 3x more expensive. About 98% of the reported 1.55 s is the bootstrap. The paper itself shows that this bootstrap gives badly under-covering bands (42.3%/58.3% at nominal 80%/95%) and replaces it with conformal bands, which cost nothing at deployment. The conclusion that all costs are negligible next to one reference analysis still holds. But the reported numbers attribute the cost to the wrong component and invert the ranking of the point forecasters. My timings come from a shared 4-core machine and are indicative only. The ratios are large enough not to depend on this.
issues.evidence: code/src/evaluation/forecast_experiment.py: t_start (line 77) to t_rpm (line 82) times RPMForecaster(n_boot=50) only, using lam_pool = truth['lam'] (line 63) computed in run_truth (line 39). t1 (line 88) to t_curve (line 90) times pilot_subsample_curve only; curve_forecast for IPL3/IPL2/EXP3/LOG2 runs after t_curve. In my recomputation (all 38 tasks, identical seeds, single-threaded BLAS) the RPM point forecast took median 0.026 s and the sub-sampling plus 4 curve fits median 0.31 s. KSSL-MIR:OC, n0 = 25/100/200: pool eigen-spectrum (12,002 x 213) 0.12 s; RPM with B = 0: 0.031-0.035 s; RPM with B = 50: 1.6-2.1 s; RPM-w with B = 50: 1.7-2.9 s. RPM-w timings in results/raw/forecasts_refine_*.csv (column t_sec, mean 1.42 s) are recorded but not reported.
issues.corrective_action: Report the run time per component and per method on identical work units: (i) the one-off eigen-decomposition of the unlabelled spectra, (ii) the RPM/RPM-w point forecast, (iii) the bootstrap bands per replicate, (iv) the within-pilot curve plus fit for IPL3, (v) FLAT/SLOPE-T plus conformal bands. Revise the sentence in Section 4.9 so that it states the point-forecast cost and the uncertainty cost separately.

issues.title: Pilot-only RPM-w ('requires only the pilot') is claimed but never evaluated; the role of unlabelled spectra is overstated
issues.description: Unlabelled spectra are presented as a key ingredient: Introduction ('unlabelled spectra are cheap, so the covariance spectrum can be estimated accurately'), Section 2.3 observation 1 and Section 3.4. Every reported RPM-w forecast (Table 2, Fig. 6, Section 4.5) uses the eigen-spectrum of the entire calibration pool, up to 12,011 unlabelled spectra for KSSL. Yet recommendation (vi) in Section 4.10 tells practitioners that 'RPM-w provides a theory-based, conservative alternative that requires only the pilot'. The paper evaluated pilot-only covariance only for unweighted RPM (and RPM-T), only at n0 in {50, 100} and only with 10 pilots (Table 3). The deployable configuration of the recommended variant is therefore untested in the paper. I ran the missing comparison myself, on the same 2,640 pilots with point forecasts. RPM-w with the pilot-only eigen-spectrum had a mean task error of 0.273 vs 0.271 with the pool spectrum (median 0.235 vs 0.246; Wilcoxon p = 0.46; pilot-only worse on 13/38 tasks). By pilot size the pilot-only/pool errors were 0.319/0.347 (n0 = 25), 0.242/0.241 (50), 0.225/0.211 (100) and 0.177/0.159 (200). The bias was more pessimistic with pilot-only spectra at every n0 (+0.075/+0.093/+0.131/+0.147 vs -0.029/+0.042/+0.090/+0.110). The claim is therefore roughly right on average. But it hides a trade-off that depends on n0, and it means that the unlabelled-spectrum component of RPM adds essentially nothing for the variant the authors recommend. Fig1_workflow.png (not included in the manuscript) still advertises 'Unlabelled spectra (cheap, many)' as an input.
issues.evidence: code/experiments/refinement.py line 59: lam = truth['lam'] (pool eigen-spectrum) for RPM-w/RPM-T/RPM-wT. Table 3 rows 'eigen-spectrum from pilot spectra only' (RPM, n0 in {50,100}, 10 pilots). Manuscript Section 4.10 (vi). Reviewer recomputation: /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R7/exp_pilotcov.py, all 38 tasks, 20 pilots per n0, seeds as in run_pilots. RPM point forecasts with the pool spectrum reproduce results/raw/forecasts_main_* exactly. At n0 = 25 the pilot eigen-spectrum has only 22-24 non-zero eigenvalues (vs 94-216 for the pool).
issues.corrective_action: Add RPM-w with the pilot-only eigen-spectrum (and with about 250 unlabelled spectra) to the main comparison for all n0 and all pilots. State explicitly which inputs the recommended configuration needs. Either tone down the 'unlabelled spectra' motivation in the Introduction and Section 2.3, or show a setting in which they help.
issues.proposed_experiment: RPM-w with pilot-only eigen-spectrum and with a 250-spectrum unlabelled set, all 38 tasks, n0 = 25-200, 20 pilots, same seeds (about 0.02 s per point forecast; well under 10 CPU-minutes without bootstrap).

issues.title: Practitioners cannot reimplement or apply RPM from the paper: settings undocumented, no user-level interface, code deposit deferred
issues.description: The manuscript does not give several settings that determine RPM's output: the penalty grid (53 log-spaced values of mu/lambda_1 from 1e-12 to 10); n_eff = n0 minus the mean group size; the eigenvalue floor (1e-14 lambda_1); the kappa root-finder (log-space bisection, 80 iterations); the optimiser (L-BFGS-B, three noise-fraction starts, box bounds of +/-25 in log scale); the fallback cut-off of 0.95 when fewer than 3 path points are valid; and the number of bootstrap replicates (B = 50 main, B = 30 robustness). The bootstrap count is mentioned only in passing in Section 4.9. Section 3.3 mentions '53-point grid' without its range. The code README documents only how to reproduce the study. There is no example of applying RPM-w, SLOPE-T or the calibrated bands to a user's own pilot. RPMForecaster.fit_forecast() needs a precomputed eigen-spectrum and an explicit horizon vector, and it assumes the SNV/sub-sampling pipeline. The Data availability statement says the code 'will be deposited in a public repository upon acceptance', so readers have no persistent, citable software. The workflow figure exists (figures/Fig1_workflow.png) but is absent from the manuscript: figure numbering starts at Fig. 2 in manuscript_full.md and Final_Manuscript.docx.
issues.evidence: code/src/models/theory.py: DEFAULT_MU_REL = np.logspace(-12, 1, 53); solve_kappa(iters=80). code/src/models/forecasters.py fit_rpm: three starts, L-BFGS-B, bounds, fallback cut-off 0.95. eigen_spectrum floor_rel=1e-14. config/full.yaml n_boot: 50; robustness n_boot: 30. A grep of manuscript_full.md and supplementary_full.md for 'logspace', '1e-12', 'L-BFGS', 'bisection' and 'optimi' returns nothing. code/README.md sections 3-7 cover only reproduction. Manuscript 'Data availability'.
issues.corrective_action: Add an algorithm box (Supplementary) listing every setting above. Archive the code now with a DOI (e.g. Zenodo) so that reviewers and readers can cite a fixed version. Add a minimal user-facing function or CLI, e.g. forecast_learning_curve(X_pilot, y_pilot, groups=None, X_unlabelled=None, n_grid, method in {'RPM-w','SLOPE-T','FLAT'}, bands='conformal'), with a runnable example on one public data set. Include the workflow figure as Fig. 1, updated to reflect the findings (unlabelled spectra optional; calibrated bands; sample-size output flagged as unreliable).

issues.title: Native spectral resolution is untested: the 5-8x wavelength thinning is unexplained, and cost and accuracy at realistic p are unknown
issues.description: All spectra were thinned before modelling to 94-216 numerically independent variables (Table 1). OSSL VisNIR was taken every 10 nm and MIR every 16 cm-1 from 2 nm / 2 cm-1 grids, Diesel every 2nd and Tablets every 3rd point. No reason is given, computational or otherwise. Routine NIR/MIR calibrations use 500-3,500 variables. The deterministic-equivalent equations (2)-(3) sum over every mode with lambda_k > 1e-14 lambda_1. At native resolution many more near-null modes enter kappa, df2 and the fitted tau^2/sigma^2 split, especially at the weakly regularised path points (mu down to 1e-12 lambda_1). The forecast therefore need not be invariant to this pre-processing choice. The paper gives neither accuracy nor run time at native resolution. On cost: the theory evaluation is O(B x H x 53 x 80 x p) and the pool eigen-decomposition is O(N p^2). My synthetic timing (see evidence) suggests this remains affordable, but it is the authors' job to show it on real spectra. A practitioner who applies RPM to full-resolution spectra is outside the validated domain.
issues.evidence: code/src/data/datasets.py OSSL_LIBS (lines 46-55): (400, 2480, 10) and (600, 4000, 16) column selection; line 202 X[:, ::2] (diesel); line 222 X[:, ::3] (tablets). Manuscript Section 3.2: 'wavelength sub-sampling to 100-220 variables' with no justification. Reviewer synthetic timing (single-threaded BLAS, shared machine, indicative): RPM point forecast 0.03 s at p = 200, 0.07 s at p = 1,000 and 0.14 s at p = 1,700. With B = 50: 1.3 / 3.7 / 6.4 s. Eigen-decomposition of 4,000 unlabelled spectra: 0.03 / 0.44 / 1.8 s. Cost therefore rises roughly linearly with p for the forecast and quadratically for the eigen-decomposition. It stays affordable, but it is not reported.
issues.corrective_action: Justify the thinning. Rerun RPM-w, SLOPE-T and FLAT, with ground truth recomputed, at native resolution on at least three tasks (e.g. ICRAF-MIR OC, KSSL-VisNIR clay, Tablets assay). Report forecast error, change versus the thinned data, and run time (eigen-decomposition, point forecast, bootstrap). Otherwise restrict the stated domain of validity to thinned spectra.
issues.proposed_experiment: Native-resolution rerun (p ~ 650-1,700) of ground truth plus RPM-w/SLOPE-T/FLAT on 3 tasks, 20 pilots per n0, with timing per component.

issues.title: Timing protocol, hardware and total compute are undocumented; timings are confounded by concurrent workers
issues.description: The timings are wall-clock (time.time()) inside 4 joblib worker processes that share the 4-core machine with the other tasks (run_all.py default --jobs = cpu_count). The manuscript calls this 'one CPU core'. CPU model and clock, BLAS library and RAM are not reported. The hardware log stores only the core count and the Python version. Table S31 pools all tasks, pilot sizes and horizons. Yet the cost of RPM is almost independent of n0 (raw means 1.43 s at n0 = 25 and 2.01 s at n0 = 200) and scales instead with B x number of horizons. The pooled numbers also carry scheduling noise. KSSL-VisNIR pilots averaged 3.21 s and KSSL-MIR pilots 1.86 s, although the two have practically identical workloads (p 208 vs 212, same 8 horizons, same pilots per n0). In my recomputation their point forecasts took 0.035 s and 0.034 s. The total compute of the study is not reported either. The run log shows the main stage took 26.7 min wall on 4 cores, the refinement about 50 min and robustness 7.6 min. This useful fact is replaced by 'several CPU-hours' in the README. Peak memory is not reported.
issues.evidence: code/run_all.py lines 60 and 80 (Parallel n_jobs = cpu_count); detect_hardware() lines 36-46. results/experiment_logs/run_full.log (start 19:20:20, end 19:47:01; refinement 14:40-15:30; robustness 457.4 s). Reviewer aggregation of the '_timing' rows in results/raw/forecasts_main_*.csv: by n0, mean t_rpm 1.434/1.352/1.571/2.010 s; by library, KSSL-VisNIR 3.205 s vs KSSL-MIR 1.858 s.
issues.corrective_action: State the CPU model and clock, RAM, BLAS and threading, and whether the timings were taken serially or under concurrent load. Re-time serially, use perf_counter or process_time, and stratify by n0, p, number of horizons and B. Give the total wall-clock and CPU time of each pipeline stage and the peak memory. Move a compact version of Table S31 into Section 4.9.

issues.title: Bootstrap bands use only B = 50 (B = 30 in robustness) and the number of replicates is not stated in the Methods
issues.description: The RPM and RPM-w uncertainty bands are quantiles of only B = 50 Bayesian-bootstrap replicates (config/full.yaml). The robustness experiments use only B = 30, which feeds the coverage column of Table 4. The 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles are thus interpolated between the 2nd and 3rd most extreme of 50 draws. Neither number appears in the Methods: B = 50 is mentioned only in passing in Section 4.9, and B = 30 not at all. A replicate costs about 0.03 s, so there is no computational reason for such a small B. I reran 6 tasks (the Table 4 set) at n0 = 25 and 100, 10 pilots each, with B = 50, which reproduces the published bands exactly, and with B = 500. The 95% bands widened (median log-width ratio B50/B500 0.92, 10th-90th percentile 0.79-1.11), and coverage rose from 56.9% to 60.0% (95%) and from 43.8% to 45.8% (80%). Most of the under-coverage is therefore systematic, as the authors say. But part of it, and a good deal of the band-to-band noise, comes from Monte-Carlo error that a negligible compute increase would remove.
issues.evidence: config/full.yaml n_boot: 50; robustness n_boot: 30. Manuscript Section 2.3 and 3.4 (no B). Reviewer check /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R7/exp_boot.py: 520 horizon-level forecasts. B = 50 bands identical to results/raw/forecasts_main_* (max |diff| = 0.0). Coverage 80%/95%: B = 50 43.8%/56.9%, B = 500 45.8%/60.0%. Median width factors 1.40/1.67 (B = 50) vs 1.44/1.72 (B = 500). Run time per pilot: B = 50 1.4 s, B = 500 13.8 s (on a shared machine).
issues.corrective_action: State B in Section 2.3/3.4. Either raise B (bootstrap replicates cost about 0.03 s each) or show that coverage is insensitive to B, and use the same B in the robustness experiments so the coverage column of Table 4 is comparable.

issues.title: The single-command reproduction fails on a clean install: statsmodels is missing from requirements.txt/environment.yml
issues.description: The analysis stage imports statsmodels to fit the slope regression behind 'R^2 = 0.73' (Section 4.2, Supplementary Table S4). statsmodels is not listed in requirements.txt or environment.yml, and none of the listed packages pulls it in. A user who follows the README will see run_all.py --stage analysis fail with ImportError. This contradicts the statement that 'a single script (run_all.py) reproduces every number'. requirements.txt is pinned but environment.yml is not, so the two install routes can produce different numerical environments.
issues.evidence: code/experiments/analysis.py line 409: import statsmodels.api as sm. code/requirements.txt (numpy, scipy, pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, joblib, pyyaml, python-docx, pytest). code/environment.yml (unpinned). Manuscript 'Data availability'.
issues.corrective_action: Add statsmodels (pinned) to both files, pin environment.yml, and verify with a clean-environment run of --mode quick in CI.

issues.title: Table 1 column 'p' is the covariance rank, not the number of spectral variables
issues.description: Table 1 defines p as 'spectral variables after sub-sampling', but the analysis code writes the length of the eigen-spectrum, i.e. the numerical rank after SNV. The actual input dimensions are 213 (MIR), 209 (VisNIR), 151 (Neospectra), 103 (Mango; the table says 94), 201 (Diesel), 217 (Tablets), 100 (Tecator) and 117 (CGL). The difference is small except for Mango. But this is the input dimension a user needs to know, and the quantity that drives cost.
issues.evidence: code/experiments/analysis.py line 290: 'p': int(len(z['lam'])). Reviewer reload of all 38 tasks with load_task(): X.shape[1] as listed above.
issues.corrective_action: Report both the number of variables and the numerical rank, and label each correctly.

recommendation_rationale: No issue undermines the core empirical findings, and computational cost is not a practical obstacle. But the paper's practical promise, a planning rule that analysts can use, is not deliverable in its current form. The calibrated band offsets are missing; the 'pilot-only' configuration of the recommended method was not evaluated; the algorithm settings and a usable software interface are absent; and the reported cost comparison is misleading. Fixing these needs one cheap experiment (pilot-only RPM-w), one moderate experiment (native resolution on a few tasks) and several reporting and software changes.
